name: Sea moss / chlorella / spirulina

card.summary: Algae powders and gels marketed as superfood skin-and-energy boosters, with no appearance trials behind them.
card.note: Contamination (microcystins, heavy metals) and iodine content are documented concerns.

quick.overview:
Sea moss (Irish moss), chlorella and spirulina are algae products sold as superfood supplements for general wellness, skin and energy.

Public health sources say evidence is insufficient to recommend them for any human condition, and no studies were found testing them for appearance.
quick.mechanism: They are nutrient-dense foods (protein, minerals, carrageenan in sea moss), and proponents attribute wider benefits to this content; published research has not established such effects.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include microcystin and heavy-metal contamination of some products, allergic reactions, drug interactions, high iodine in sea moss, and FDA warning letters over false health claims for chlorella products.

lead: Sea moss, chlorella and spirulina are algae-based products sold as dietary supplements and 'superfoods'. Sea moss usually refers to Irish moss (Chondrus crispus), a red seaweed of North Atlantic coasts rich in the thickener carrageenan, often prepared as a gel.[1] Chlorella is a genus of single-celled green algae,[2] and spirulina is the dried biomass of cyanobacteria, mainly of the genus Arthrospira.[3]

They are used in wellness and appearance-oriented circles as a nutrient-dense route to clearer, healthier-looking skin, more energy and better recovery. Sea moss in particular is promoted on social media with 'cleared my skin' testimonials, which looksmax.org users discuss with some skepticism. Their protein, minerals, iodine and antioxidant pigments are the reasons proponents give.[1][3]

Research is mixed in scope. A 2023 narrative review of nutritional supplements for skin health analysed 14 compounds including chlorella and spirulina and described possible photoprotective and anti-inflammatory benefits for skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis and psoriasis.[4] Small randomized trials have examined chlorella for antioxidant status, cycling performance and detoxification markers,[5][6][7] while public health bodies have not endorsed these products for any condition: the NIH has said the evidence is insufficient to recommend spirulina for any human condition, and the American Cancer Society has said available studies do not support chlorella for preventing or treating disease.[2][3]

chain: Algae supply protein, minerals and antioxidant pigments
Proponents expect better skin health and recovery
Clearer-looking skin and more training energy
angle.text: Users take sea moss gel, chlorella tablets or spirulina powder as a food-based way to support skin and energy. A review of skin-health supplements includes chlorella and spirulina among compounds with possible skin benefits.

paras: Irish moss is a red alga whose dry weight is roughly 55 percent carrageenan, with protein, minerals and notable iodine and sulfur content. When boiled it forms a gel that can hold many times its weight in water, and it has long been used in puddings in Scotland and Ireland, while carrageenan is an industrial food thickener.[1]

Spirulina has been harvested historically, for example by the Aztecs from Lake Texcoco and by the Kanembu people near Lake Chad, with large-scale production studied from the 1970s.[3] Dried spirulina is high in protein, but its vitamin B12 is mostly an inactive form, and the American Dietetic Association (2009) said it is not a reliable B12 source.[3] Chlorella was promoted in the mid-twentieth century as a solution to world hunger, but its indigestible cell wall and low energy capture limited that idea, and it has since been sold mainly as a health food.[2] A 2016 review of microalgae nutraceuticals describes spirulina and chlorella as the main marketed strains, followed by Klamath, and discusses quality control of marketed products.[8]

A 2023 review of nutritional supplements for skin health covered vitamins A, C, D and E, omega-3, biotin, astaxanthin and others alongside chlorella and spirulina, and reported that each showed some possible benefit for skin condition, including photoprotection and a positive influence on inflammatory skin diseases.[4]
Looksmax.org users discuss sea moss mostly through TikTok testimonials about clearer skin, with one poster doubting those claims.[9]

Because recovery feeds into training, athletic studies are relevant to the physique angle. A randomized crossover trial of chlorella in trained cyclists measured endurance, time trial and lactate threshold,[7] another in young healthy adults reported lower blood lactate and higher oxygen pulse during cycling,[10] and a 2023 trial examined whether algae ingestion changes muscle protein synthesis in young adults compared with mycoprotein.[11] Six weeks of chlorella improved antioxidant status in Korean male smokers in a trial.[5]

Some cyanobacteria produce toxins called microcystins. Spirulina does not make them, but contaminated batches can contain them, and Health Canada set a limit for microcystin-LR in finished products. Heavy-metal contamination of some spirulina products, including lead, has also been reported.[3] Spirulina may interact with immune-related or blood-clotting medications and contains phenylalanine, and a 2024 review identified a small number of allergy cases including anaphylaxis.[3]

Chlorella cell walls have been reported to contain lipopolysaccharides that may affect the immune system, although later work suggests these differ from those of Gram-negative bacteria.[2] The US FDA has issued warning letters to supplement companies for falsely advertising health benefits of chlorella products.[2] Sea moss is rich in iodine, and available sources do not give intake guidance;[1] a poster on looksmax.org said it caused thyroid problems for a friend.[9]

No studies found examining sea moss, chlorella or spirulina specifically for facial appearance. Human trials of chlorella include a randomized crossover study in 14 trained male cyclists,[7] a trial of oxidative stress markers in senior Japanese subjects,[12] a six-week trial in Korean male smokers,[5] and a small placebo-controlled crossover study of chlorella and heterocyclic amine detoxification.[6] The European Food Safety Authority rejected claimed blood-glucose benefits of spirulina in 2013, and HIV studies found no conclusive effect on mortality, weight or immune response.[3]
